extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing novelists, serious students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing long-form novels: choosing a single subject, shaping material so form and matter coincide, handling scale/space/time, and keeping narrative method and point of view consistent. Emphasis on diagnosing failures of form (illustrated by War and Peace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must express the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form is that which makes the most of its subject—there is no other definition of the meaning of form in fiction. The well-made book is the book in which the subject and the form coincide and are indistinguishable—the book in which the matter is all used up in the form, in which the form expresses all the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the structure of the novel so that every formal choice serves the subject; if form and matter disagree, material will be superfluous or wanting. Example/anti-pattern: Tolstoy’s War and Peace shows magnificent material but a form that does not wholly express the central subject, producing loss to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must be single and concise
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject, one and whole and irreducible—a novel cannot begin to take shape till it has this for its support. If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to state the novel’s unifying subject succinctly (ten words or so). Use that phrase as the organizing principle for selection and arrangement of material; inability to name a subject indicates lack of firm basis for form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and presence of a centre
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of a book needs a centre; where there is no centre the general shape of the novel fails to satisfy the eye. A confusion of two designs (i.e., two centres) masks coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the novel has a dominant organising idea or focal centre. Avoid accidentally writing two novels at once; if multiple large themes are present, either deliberately couple them with a unifying scheme or separate into distinct works. The War and Peace example: alternation between 'youth and age' and 'war and peace' produces lack of a single centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material—avoid wastefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy’s novel is wasteful of its subject; the story is damaged by the importation of another and an irrelevant story—waste of material undermines the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune or reassign material that does not directly advance or illuminate the chosen subject. Superfluous sequences or an imported subplot dilute the book’s power; every scene should contribute to the central design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent narrative method and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominant point of view should be coherent. Tolstoy alternates between telling the story himself (authorial narration) and letting characters’ consciousnesses carry the effect; the inconsistency produces different principles governing parts of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and sustain a narrative method (e.g., free indirect discourse centered on characters, or an authorial narrator) unless shifts are motivated and patterned. Anti-patterns include choosing an onlooker 'at random' or switching viewpoint without a principled reason—such shifts break the unity of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial digressions and pamphleteering
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid interminable chapters of comment and explanation, chapters in the manner of a controversial pamphlet (e.g., Tolstoy’s historical/theoretical interruptions), which interrupt the fictional action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep expository or theoretical argument out of the novel’s narrative flow unless it is deliberately integrated; long authorial lectures encourage readers to skip and damage immersion. If historical/theoretical material is essential, embed it via character perspective or a separate, clearly signposted device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of time must be structural
rubrics_metrics.description: If time is of the essence, the form of time is to be represented, and that is something more than to represent its contents in their order. Merely to lengthen the series of stages will not ensure perception of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the passage of time perceptible through the build and shape of the book (arrangement of stages, echoes, contrasts, pacing), not by summary lines like 'years have fled.' Ensure the novel’s lines and masses show the wheel of time turning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale, cast, and openness for the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects such as the march of life require a generous amount of room for their needs: a big and various population, a sense of a wide world opening away from the centre. The effect of a wide world must be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match scope and number of characters, scenes, and settings to the ambition of the subject. For an idea of universality, supply enough representative figures and peripheral life so protagonists appear part of a larger continuum rather than isolated exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a convincing sense of space and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity of space and of daylight is essential to some motives; Tolstoy’s people move in an atmosphere that knows no limit—the horizon is vague and vast—producing a sense that life continues beyond the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques (selective naming, off-stage action, consistent atmosphere, references to expanses) to suggest a world beyond the scenes. Contrastive choices (e.g., Dostoevsky’s enclosed darkness) are deliberate stylistic options—choose the spatial effect that suits the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should serve the novel’s representative purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose figures for their capacity to embody the novel’s central idea: 'They illustrate the story that is the same always and everywhere... Essentially they are not princes, not Russians, but figures in the great procession.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for universality, select and shape characters so they stand as types or embodiments of the theme rather than merely historical or local exemplars. If particularity is the aim, make their conditions integral to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and finish of parts—each part must be lucid and shapely
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-composed novel shows lucidity and shapeliness in its parts; there is no faltering in his hold upon character; each episode should not betray a hesitating intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the composition and finish of individual scenes and episodes: clarity of intention, proportionate treatment, and integration into the larger form. Parts that are 'mutilated' or fragmentary hurt the overall design; ensure sufficient grouping and composition of major cycles within the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of development and avoidance of contradictory turns
rubrics_metrics.description: At any point one must ask: Is this proceeding of the author the right one, the best for the subject? Does the treatment diverge from the line of its true development? Unexpected turns that contradict the subject indicate flawed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly check whether narrative developments serve the central subject. Avoid divergences that cannot be justified as deepening or unifying the theme; readers reconstruct the author’s labour and will judge choices—maintain purposeful direction.
